## 28.1 Bivariate Choropleth Maps

Bivariate choropleth maps encode two variables simultaneously using a 3×3 or 4×4 color grid, revealing the spatial co-occurrence of paired phenomena. For rural health analysis, classical bivariate maps show the joint distribution of poverty and uninsurance, provider shortage and adverse outcomes, or access score and disease burden. These maps are analytically powerful because they reveal whether high-need areas (high disease burden) are also low-resource areas (low provider supply) — the defining characteristic of a healthcare desert.

```julia
# === Bivariate choropleth mapping in GeoMakie.jl ===
using GeoMakie, CairoMakie, Statistics
"""
bivariate_map(geoms, var1, var2;
title1, title2, outfile, k=3)
```

Create a bivariate choropleth map encoding two variables as a k×k color matrix.

Standard k=3 gives a 9-color 3×3 grid (Steven's bivariate scheme).

```julia
# Color encoding (3×3 example):
#   Low-Low (var1 low, var2 low) = light grey
#   High-High (both high) = dark purple
#   High var1 only = blue; High var2 only = orange
"""
function bivariate_map(
geoms,
var1::Vector{Float64},
var2::Vector{Float64};
title1::String = "Variable 1",
title2::String = "Variable 2",
outfile::String = "bivariate_map.pdf",
k::Int = 3,
projection::String = "+proj=laea +lat_0=45 +lon_0=-96"
)
# ── Classify each variable into k quantile classes ────────
classify_quantile(v, k) = begin
q = quantile(v, range(0, 1; length=k+1))
[searchsortedfirst(q, vi) |> x -> min(x, k) for vi in v]
end
c1 = classify_quantile(var1, k)  # 1..k
c2 = classify_quantile(var2, k)  # 1..k
# ── Build bivariate color palette ─────────────────────────
# Joshua Stevens bivariate palette (3×3): row=var1, col=var2
bivariate_palette_3x3 = [
"#e8e8e8" "#ace4e4" "#5ac8c8";   # Low var1
"#dfb0d6" "#a5add3" "#5698b9";   # Mid var1
"#be64ac" "#8c62aa" "#3b4994"    # High var1
]
color_for(i1, i2) = parse(RGBf, bivariate_palette_3x3[i1, i2])
colors = [color_for(c1[i], c2[i]) for i in 1:length(geoms)]
# ── Draw map ──────────────────────────────────────────────
fig = Figure(resolution=(1400, 900))
ax  = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1];
dest  = projection,
title = "Bivariate: $(title1) × $(title2)",
titlefont = :bold)
poly!(ax, geoms; color=colors, strokecolor=:white, strokewidth=0.3)
# ── Draw bivariate legend ─────────────────────────────────
ax_legend = Axis(fig[1, 2];
width=100, height=100,
xlabel=title1, ylabel=title2,
xlabelsize=11, ylabelsize=11,
aspect=1)
for r in 1:k, c in 1:k
poly!(ax_legend,
```

Rect((r-1)/k, (c-1)/k, 1/k, 1/k);

color=parse(RGBf, bivariate_palette_3x3[r,c]),

strokecolor=:white, strokewidth=0.5)


## 28.2 Dot Density Maps for Rural Population Distribution

```julia

hidedecorations!(ax_legend; label=false)
save(outfile, fig; pt_per_unit=1)

```

Dot density maps represent population by placing one dot for every N people, randomly distributed within each geographic unit. They avoid the perceptual distortion of choropleth maps where large rural counties appear more important than small dense urban ones. For rural health analysis, dot density maps are ideal for showing where population is actually located relative to healthcare facilities, because they correctly represent the sparseness of rural populations.

```julia
# === Dot density map generation ===
using GeoMakie, CairoMakie, Random, GeoInterface
"""
dot_density_map(geoms, populations;
dots_per_person=1000, rng=MersenneTwister(42))
```

Generate random dot positions for dot density map.

Each dot represents dots_per_person people.

Dots are uniformly distributed within each polygon's bounding box

then filtered to inside the polygon.

"""


## 28.3 Cartogram Generation

```julia
function dot_density_map(
geoms,
populations::Vector{<:Real};
dots_per_person::Int = 1000,
rng::AbstractRNG     = MersenneTwister(42),
projection::String   = "+proj=laea +lat_0=45 +lon_0=-96",
dot_color            = :navy,
dot_size::Float64    = 1.5,
outfile::String      = "dot_density.pdf"
)
all_x = Float64[]
all_y = Float64[]
for (geom, pop) in zip(geoms, populations)
n_dots = max(1, round(Int, pop / dots_per_person))
coords = GeoInterface.coordinates(geom)
# Bounding box for rejection sampling
all_coords = [pt for ring in coords for pt in ring]
xs = [c[1] for c in all_coords]
ys = [c[2] for c in all_coords]
xmin, xmax = extrema(xs)
ymin, ymax = extrema(ys)
placed = 0
attempts = 0
max_attempts = n_dots * 20  # Safety limit
while placed < n_dots && attempts < max_attempts
px = xmin + rand(rng) * (xmax - xmin)
py = ymin + rand(rng) * (ymax - ymin)
# Test if point is inside polygon (ray casting)
if GeoInterface.contains(geom, GeoInterface.Point([px, py]))
push!(all_x, px)
push!(all_y, py)
placed += 1
end
attempts += 1
end
end
# Draw map
fig = Figure(resolution=(1400, 900))
ax  = GeoAxis(fig[1,1]; dest=projection,
title="Population Dot Density (1 dot = $(dots_per_person) people)")
poly!(ax, geoms; color=:white, strokecolor=:grey60, strokewidth=0.3)
scatter!(ax, all_x, all_y;
color=dot_color, markersize=dot_size, alpha=0.6)
save(outfile, fig; pt_per_unit=1)
@info "$(length(all_x)) dots placed in $(outfile)"
end
```

Cartograms distort geographic area in proportion to a data variable — population, disease burden, or healthcare spending. They correct the visual bias of standard maps where large rural counties dominate the display despite having fewer people. Two cartogram algorithms are widely used: the Gastner-Newman diffusion cartogram (continuous, requires PDE solver) and the Dorling cartogram (non-overlapping circles scaled by variable). Julia implements the Dorling cartogram through iterative circle placement.

```julia
# === Dorling cartogram: non-overlapping circles scaled by population ===
using LinearAlgebra
"""
dorling_cartogram(centroids, values, geoms;
iterations=100, friction=0.25)
```

Compute Dorling cartogram positions using iterative force-directed layout.

Circle areas are proportional to `values` (e.g. county population).

Returns updated centroid positions after circle overlap resolution.

"""

```julia
function dorling_cartogram(
centroids::Matrix{Float64},  # n×2 [x y] centroid positions
values::Vector{Float64},
geoms;
iterations::Int    = 100,
friction::Float64  = 0.25,
max_radius::Float64 = nothing
)
n    = size(centroids, 1)
# Radius proportional to sqrt(value) (area ∝ value)
scale = isnothing(max_radius) ?
0.4 * mean(norm.(eachrow(diff(extrema(centroids; dims=1)[1], extrema(centroids;dims=1)[2])))) / sqrt(maximum(values)) :
max_radius / sqrt(maximum(values))
radii = scale .* sqrt.(values)
pos   = copy(centroids)  # Mutable positions
vel   = zeros(n, 2)      # Velocities
for iter in 1:iterations
forces = zeros(n, 2)
for i in 1:n
for j in (i+1):n
dx    = pos[i,1] - pos[j,1]
dy    = pos[i,2] - pos[j,2]
dist  = sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2)
r_sum = radii[i] + radii[j]
if dist < r_sum && dist > 1e-10
# Repulsion force proportional to overlap
overlap   = r_sum - dist
magnitude = overlap / dist
forces[i,1] += magnitude * dx
forces[i,2] += magnitude * dy
forces[j,1] -= magnitude * dx
forces[j,2] -= magnitude * dy
end
end
# Attraction toward original centroid (prevents drift)
forces[i,1] += friction * (centroids[i,1] - pos[i,1])
forces[i,2] += friction * (centroids[i,2] - pos[i,2])
end
# Damped velocity update
vel  .= 0.5 .* vel .+ forces
pos  .+= 0.1 .* vel
end
return (positions=pos, radii=radii)
end
```
